title: Differentiation I: Product Differentiation
keyQuestion: Is what the company sees as value-add recognized and rewarded by customers?

reading.name: Differentiation: what it is, where WTP comes from, how to tell whether you have it, and how fast it decays (brief)

slides: S9 deck 'Differentiation Advantage' (40; title slide reads STRAT 392): strategy canvas and four actions (Cirque, Wii, Airbnb), jobs to be done, consumption chain, segmentation, NPS, consumer surplus, price discrimination, Ferrari profit per car

framework.name: Differentiation on the value stick
framework.summary: Being different is not differentiation. Differentiation is the ability to raise what a buyer will pay by more than it costs to create the reason they pay. It counts only if the buyer both perceives it and pays (or is willing to pay) for it. The definitive test is a realized price premium, and it has a signature in the accounts.

components.name: The value stick
components.what: Four levels: supplier opportunity cost (what a supplier would accept), cost, price, willingness to pay. Value created = WTP − supplier opportunity cost. Price splits it: customer surplus (WTP − price), firm margin (price − cost), supplier surplus (cost − supplier opportunity cost). Differentiation moves the top; cost leadership moves the bottom; only the first creates the option to charge more.

components.name: Six sources of WTP
components.what: Performance (TSMC node lead), risk reduction (Old Dominion: 42% more per cwt, 99% on time, 0.1% claims), time and convenience (+1.45% online sales per business day cut), switching and integration (NVIDIA 7.5M developers), identity and signal (Hermès 41.0% vs. Kering 12.8% operating margin), trust in a market the buyer can't verify (auto repair).

components.name: Search/experience/credence goods
components.what: Normal goods: quality knowable before/after purchase; experience goods: only after; credence goods: never known (medical, legal, repair). For credence goods differentiation can't be demonstrated, only signaled.

components.name: Six tests for a premium
components.what: Price (realized vs. a matched competitor, not list); volume at parity; elasticity (price rise accepted at the shelf, not in a survey); retention (tracks satisfaction, not switching cost); mix (attach rate of higher-margin options); where it lands (gain in price = differentiation; gain entirely in cost = an operating improvement).

components.name: Differentiation decays
components.what: US non-financials 1970-2024: average annual ROIC fade 0.21 (consumer staples 0.10, health care 0.18, IT 0.20, energy 0.29, utilities 0.30); market-implied advantage periods 5-20 years; Wiggins & Ruefli: superior performance rarely persists. Lululemon gross margin 59.2 → 56.6 → 54.2%.

components.name: Five ways it fails
components.what: The buyer didn't want the attribute (JCPenney fair pricing); copied before it could pay (Casper, ~175 bed-in-a-box brands); matching a rival broke the profit formula (Blockbuster ending late fees); the feature was real and nobody would pay (Fire Phone); the premium didn't survive normalization (Peloton).

components.name: Four durability mechanisms
components.what: Path dependence, causal ambiguity, social complexity, credible commitment (a rival could match the promise but won't surrender the option needed to make it believable — guarantees, irrevocable governance, posted pricing rules). A differentiator resting on none of the four is a routine, and routines travel.

components.name: Six-step diagnostic
components.what: 1) Name the buyer and the alternative. 2) State the premium as a realized number. 3) Name which of the six sources produces it and whether the buyer can verify it or must be given a signal. 4) Name which durability mechanism prevents imitation. 5) Check where the gain lands. 6) Ask what would make the premium gone in five years; falling gross margin at constant mix is usually the first signal.

components.name: Tools to find differentiation (slides)
components.what: Strategy canvas and the four actions (eliminate, reduce, raise, create); jobs to be done; mapping the consumption chain; customer segmentation.

terms.def: Brief: the ability to raise what a buyer will pay by more than it costs to create the reason. Slides: offering value not available elsewhere or that others don't do as well; providing unique value that commands a premium price.
The most a buyer would pay; the top of the value stick.
What a supplier would accept; the bottom of the value stick.

The firm holds a share of profit its share of volume doesn't explain, or raises price without losing volume (Apple ~21% of units, ~49% of revenue; Ferrari shipments −3.7%, car and parts revenue +8.0%).
A good whose quality is never known even after use; differentiation must be signaled.
Part of brand equity that is a rent on buyer ignorance (pharmacists buy national-brand remedies 9% vs. 26% for average consumers); erodes as information improves.
A promise structured so the firm can't walk it back; competitors can say the words but can't sign the document.
Plot of offering levels across competing factors; blue-ocean players diverge (raise/create some factors, eliminate/reduce others) and show peaks and valleys, not a flat line.
Eliminate (factors the industry takes for granted), reduce (well below standard), raise (well above standard), create (never offered).
What the customer 'hires' a product to do; differentiation sources: does a job better, does more jobs, does a unique job, better quality/reliability, more convenient, brand/image.

Every step of the customer's experience: awareness (Listerine), finding (Coke), selecting (Uber), ordering/purchasing (Dollar Shave Club), delivery/installation and payment (RC Willey), storage/moving (Little Giant ladders), help in use (Butterball), returns/exchange (Nordstrom/Zappos), repair/disposal (Patagonia Worn Wear).
Grouping customers by similar needs — by product attributes, customer demographics, or job to be done (Christensen & Raynor).
'How likely are you to recommend us?' 9-10 promoters, 7-8 passive, 1-6 detractors; NPS = % promoters − % detractors.
Value customers obtain by buying for less than they'd be willing to pay; the area under the demand curve above price.

Charging higher prices to consumers with higher WTP: 1st degree (each customer's reservation price — auctions), 2nd degree (by quantity — bulk discounts), 3rd degree (by group — student/senior, business/economy).

claims.claim: A firm can be unmistakably different and earn nothing — the ordinary fate of most features — and nearly indistinguishable yet command a premium.

Any WTP figure quoted without naming a product and a price point is close to meaningless: the same fair-trade label held an 8% price rise on one coffee (elasticity 0.28) and lost ~30% volume on another for 9% (−3.32).
Survey-based WTP has no budget constraint; act on field experiments and purchase records.
Durability does not come from the attribute; it comes from why a competitor cannot supply the same attribute at the same cost.
If profits improved without any price moving, the achievement was in cost, and cost achievements diffuse.

Spending customers cannot perceive is philanthropy toward suppliers; a credible proxy is often worth more than the underlying quality (and the premium harvest — trim invisible spending, keep the price — works until it doesn't).
Chipotle's rivals are a market test: every rival invests in the freshness customers can SEE; none matches the sourcing standards customers must take on faith.

failures.name: The buyer did not want the attribute
failures.what: JCPenney 2012: net sales $17,260M → $12,985M, comps −25.2%, loss $985M; 'did not resonate with our customers.'

failures.name: Copied before it could pay
failures.what: Casper: IPO $12 (Feb 2020), taken private at $6.90 (Jan 2022); the barrier to copying was a website.

failures.name: Matching a rival broke the profit formula
failures.what: Blockbuster ended late fees (worth $250-300M operating income) in 2005, lost $588M, reinstated in 2010, bankrupt 206 days later.

failures.name: Nobody would pay for the feature
failures.what: Fire Phone $199 → $0.99 in six weeks; $170M charge.

failures.name: Premium didn't survive normalization
failures.what: Peloton bike $2,245 → $1,495 in under a year; revenue −39% from peak; first profit from subscriptions at 71.1% gross margin.

caseFacts.fact: 2025: revenue $11.92B, 4,056 restaurants, net income $1.54B, restaurant-level margin 25.4% (from 26.7%), operating margin 16.2%; comparable sales −1.7% (first decline since the crisis years); management guided flat comps for 2026 while opening 350+ restaurants a year.
caseFacts.why: The squeeze: price lever spent after ~20% cumulative increases 2021-24.

caseFacts.fact: Food, beverage and packaging 29.6% of revenue (~$3.5B); each 100 bps ≈ $120M of operating profit — close to a tenth of earnings.
caseFacts.why: The arithmetic that makes cutting tempting.

caseFacts.fact: Differentiation choices: responsibly raised meats (pulled carnitas from a third of stores in 2015 over an audit), 53 whole ingredients, fresh daily prep in view, short menu/assembly line, no franchising, digital second line and Chipotlanes (digital 36.7% of food & beverage revenue).
caseFacts.why: Some are visible at purchase (prep, line, portions); some must be taken on faith (sourcing).

caseFacts.fact: WTP evidence: ~20% cumulative price increases 2021-24 while transactions still grew; AUV ~$3.1-3.2M (roughly double typical franchised QSR); restaurant margins 25-27%; Papa John's ~5% operating margin despite also claiming ingredient superiority.
caseFacts.why: The cleanest test of WTP (price rose, volume held) — and the comparison set shows a claim alone earns nothing.

caseFacts.fact: 2015-16 food-safety crisis: comps −20.4%, net income $476M → $23M, restaurant margin 26.1% → 12.8%.
caseFacts.why: A company that charges for superior quality has made a promise every daily operation can break (trust as a WTP source cuts both ways).

caseFacts.fact: 2024 'skimpflation' backlash: customers filmed bowls; management recommitted to generous portions at a cost in margin.
caseFacts.why: Customers police the visible offer instantly — they watch the bowl, not the chicken certification.

caseFacts.fact: Rivals (Qdoba ~750 franchised units with free queso/guac; Cafe Rio and Costa Vida tortillas pressed in view with commissary prep and conventional sourcing; Moe's; Cava) signal freshness while spending less.
caseFacts.why: Evidence that the visible half of the bundle may carry most of the WTP.

caseFacts.fact: Boatwright's options: relax sourcing ($150-300M, not visible, brand-identity risk); commissary prep ($100-200M, mostly not visible); trim portions ~5% (~$175M, visible immediately, highest detection risk); substitute ingredients ($50-150M, rarely visible); cut elsewhere ($50-100M); reframe standards as value (negative savings; makes the invisible visible).
caseFacts.why: The decision expressed as visibility × risk.

strongAnalysis: Apply the brief's diagnostic: buyer = fast-casual diner choosing Chipotle vs. Qdoba/Cava; premium = realized menu price above rivals, proven by 2021-24 price increases with growing traffic; sources = performance (taste/freshness) and trust (food integrity — partly credence, so it must be signaled); durability = social complexity and credible commitment (company-owned execution, public sourcing standards).

Answer the Key Question by splitting the bundle: the VISIBLE value-adds (fresh prep, the line, portion size, speed) are clearly recognized and rewarded — customers police them. The INVISIBLE ones (responsibly raised protein, some of the 53-ingredient purity) are recognized only as brand belief; the rivals' success with conventional sourcing suggests they carry less WTP directly, but they underwrite the trust claim and the crisis showed how much that trust is worth.

Recommendation logic: don't trim what customers can see (portions — highest detection risk); be wary of 'premium harvest' on invisible sourcing (Porter §4: works beautifully until it doesn't); the stronger play is to make the invisible visible (reframe standards as value) or cut costs elsewhere — and acknowledge WTP has a ceiling (2025 counter-evidence).
Connect to the value stick: cutting invisible cost moves the bottom (a cost move); if it erodes the trust that holds WTP up, it lowers the top more than it lowers the bottom.

counter.argument: Customers can't see sourcing, rivals prove they don't pay for it, and each 100 bps is $120M. Cutting invisible costs is just good management — the premium lives in perception, which would survive intact.
counter.response: Concede the visible/invisible split is real, then point to the mechanism: Chipotle's premium rests on a credible commitment to food integrity; for a credence-like attribute the signal is the commitment itself. The 2015-16 crisis (net income $476M → $23M) shows the downside when the claim is breached, and audits, employees and media make quiet cuts discoverable. 'Premium harvest' produces several excellent years and then erosion that is very hard to reverse (Porter §4). Test before you cut: run the six premium tests and watch gross margin at constant mix.

courseMap.text: Differentiation moves the top of the value stick, the counterpart of the cost modules (S7-S8); its durability mechanisms echo VRIO's imitability barriers (S6) plus credible commitment; beyond-product differentiation (S10) and dual advantage (S11) build on it. Generic strategies: a differentiator must hold cost proximity (S1).

slideExtras.detail: Cirque du Soleil — eliminated animal shows, star performers, multiple arenas; reduced humor and thrills; raised unique venue; created artistic theme, refined environment, multiple productions. Nintendo Wii — eliminated graphics arms race, complex controllers; reduced processing power, hardcore focus, price; raised family appeal, ease of use, social gaming; created motion control, active play, multi-generational appeal. Airbnb — eliminated standardized rooms, hotel infrastructure; reduced service levels, room service, uniformity; raised local authenticity, unique properties, home amenities; created peer-to-peer platform, experiential travel, neighborhood immersion, host reviews.
13,752 cars (capped below demand), revenue €6.7B (~$525k per car), EBIT €1.9B (28%), ~$149,000 profit per car ≈ 70 GM vehicles of profit; Porsche ~$18k, BMW ~$5k, Toyota ~$3k, GM ~$2k.
Sketch a price/quality map: Wendy's, Seven Brothers, Smashburger, JCW's, In-N-Out, McDonald's, Carl's Jr., Five Guys, Cubby's, CHOM.
The supply chain (business arena) meets the consumption chain (customer arena): product receipt, unpacking, usage, storage, discard.
